entry.hook: Yazi (a dragon-born Yao who embodies the law of tooth-for-tooth) was not born seeking power, nor glory, nor even survival. He was born with one purpose only: to remember every wound, and to return it. In a cosmos that preaches forgiveness, he became the god of revenge.

body.body_1:
睚眦 / Yazi
Original Form: Jackal-headed Dragon (豺首龙身), the Second-born of the Nine Sons of the Dragon.
Birth Era: The Honghuang Era (洪荒纪元)
Shapeshifted Form: He retains his jackal-headed dragon-bodied form as his primary shape, a form that never deviates from the perfect predator. There is no record of him taking a fully human shape; his beast-body is his truest and most legible statement.
body.body_2: Current Realm: Yao Saint (妖圣). Yazi has transcended the bindings of will-torture, bloodline atavism, and the tribulations of form-making. He has existed long enough to witness the birth and death of empires. Yet the Yao Saint's ultimate emptiness is not a philosophic question for him — it is a plain fact. There is no higher order that will not call him a beast. There is no heaven that will seat him as an equal. He has power enough to shatter mountains, yet he remains, in the eyes of the cosmos, a monster. His bottleneck is not one of cultivation but of belonging: there is no throne for a vengeful dragon in any celestial court, and he refuses to beg for one.
body.body_3:
Yazi was not created by accident. He was born from the Dragon King himself — a trueborn son of the First Dragon of the Eastern Sea, carrying the full weight of the ancient progenitor's bloodline. His awakening to sentience was not a slow, painful crawl from beast to man. Among the primal brood of the Dragon's Nine Sons, Yazi was the first to know hate.

The wound that defined him came early. As a cub, he devoured a celestial fruit his father had hoarded for millennia. The Dragon King did not reason with him, did not explain the fruit's significance. He struck. The blow shattered one of Yazi's horns and left a scar across his skull that never healed — not because the flesh could not mend, but because Yazi chose to keep it.

In that moment, he learned what he was. He was not a son. He was not an heir. He was a creature that could be broken for taking what it wanted. And he decided, in the single most lucid instant of his young life, that he would never forgive.

From that day forward, Yazi never looked his father in the eye. The silence between them was heavier than any storm. The other dragon-brothers — the tortoise-backed Bixi, the music-loving Suanni — tried to mend the rift. They failed. Yazi had closed himself behind a wall that no word of apology could breach. He was alone not because he had no kin, but because he had chosen the one thing his kin could not give him: a permanent, unyielding grudge.
body.body_4:
Yazi's core formation was not a matter of cannibalizing beasts or seizing lunar essence. He is the son of a god — a direct descendant of the Dragon King, a being whose blood already hums with primordial power. The Dragon lineage does not stumble blindly into the wild. Yazi's Yao Dan (妖丹) was forged from the natural draining of his father's territory — the residual energy of the Eastern Sea's dragon veins, absorbed into his marrow from the moment of his birth. It was never a struggle for survival. It was a birthright.

But that is precisely what makes it a different kind of wound. The power was given — the grudge was earned. His core is as stable as dragon bone, as pure as deep-sea pressure. It has never threatened to explode. And that, in a strange way, is its own curse: he cannot blame his volatility on an unstable core. Every act of violence he commits is fully and solely his own choice.
body.body_5:
Yazi did not undergo the traditional Hua Xing. He is a dragon-born entity, not a creature that crawled from the mud and clawed its way toward a human shape. The Dragon King's sons are born in forms that are already legible to Heaven — dragon-bodied, jackal-headed, scaled and crowned with horns. They are never required to dissolve their bones and rebuild them as a man's skeleton.

Yet Yazi's form is a form of vengeance itself. His jackal head is not a humanizing feature — it is a warning. The sharp snout, the eyes that miss nothing, the teeth that are always slightly bared. In later ages, when human smiths began carving his likeness onto swords and shields, they did not need to imagine him. They had seen him in the memory of every blade that had tasted blood.
body.body_6:
Yazi's bloodline is not a trace of some ancient beast lost to time. It is the Dragon King himself — the firstborn of the Eastern Sea, the progenitor of an entire aquatic dynasty, a being whose authority was older than the Celestial Bureaucracy. To awaken Yazi's bloodline is to remember nothing that needs remembering, because it has never slept.

There is no ancient ancestor lurking within him, no will from the Honghuang Era that seeks to seize his body through Duo She. The risk of atavism for a trueborn dragon-born is near zero. His power does not come with the cost of ancestral possession.

But this too is a form of isolation. Other yao must fight their own blood for control, and in that struggle, they are never truly alone — their ancestor is always with them even if the presence is a threat. Yazi has nothing but himself. No ghost in his marrow. No voice in his blood. Only his own cold, calculated, endless grudge.
body.body_7:
Yazi's core obsession is singular: revenge. Not as a burst of passion, not as a heat-of-battle anger, but as a lifelong project. The tradition portrays him as a being for whom every slight, no matter how small, is recorded in a ledger that never closes. A disrespectful glance, a careless word — these are not forgotten. They are filed, cataloged, and one day, without warning, collected.

The wound from his father crystallized this pattern. Yazi was not born vengeful — he was made so by a single act of cruelty from the one being he should have been able to trust. Within the classic telling, this is the unhealable fracture. The son of the Dragon King does not forgive his father, not because he is too proud, but because forgiveness would mean that the original wound did not matter. And Yazi's entire existence is built on the premise that it did.

His tragedy is that this obsession leaves no room for anything else. He does not love. He does not seek companionship. He does not build. He is pure reaction — a living mirror held up to the world's cruelty, reflecting it back with interest. There is no peace for him because peace would be a betrayal of the one truth he has staked his life on: that every injury deserves an answer.
body.body_8:
Yazi's relationships with the four categories of existence are defined almost entirely by his function as a god of blades.

(1) With the Immortal Dao: Yazi is not hunted. He is too powerful, too well-connected by his dragon lineage, and too useful. The immortals do not seek his Yao Dan — they seek his blessing on their weapons. A sword carved in the likeness of Yazi is a sword that carries his essence of retribution.

(2) With the Divine Dao: The Heavenly Court did not try to suppress Yazi. They absorbed him. He was granted the title of "God of Blades and Swords" (刀剑之神), a celestial office that formalized his connection to edged weapons. This is not a position of honor — it is a containment strategy. By giving him a defined role, Heaven ensures that his wild vengeance is channeled into an acceptable form: the decoration of weapons that will be used in sanctioned wars, not personal grudges.

(3) With Mortal Humans: Yazi has no love for humans, but he has become their most enduring symbol of martial ferocity. From the Han dynasty onward, smiths have carved his image onto sword hilts, scabbards, and shield bosses. The belief was that a blade bearing Yazi's visage would become irresistible in battle — that the weapon itself would acquire the dragon-born's thirst for blood. Emperors commissioned swords with Yazi's form as a statement: I do not forgive. I do not forget. I am as terrible as the dragon's wrath.

(4) With His Own Kind: Yazi is a son of the Dragon, but he is distant from his siblings. The other eight sons — each with their own distinct natures — regard him with wariness. He is the brother who remembers every unkindness. There is no alliance, no brotherhood. Only the cold, careful distance that comes from knowing that any slight may be repaid.
body.body_9:
Yazi has no fixed lair. He is a guardian without a temple, a god whose altar is the blade itself. He drifts between the Dragon King's underwater palace — where he never looks his father in the eye — and the armories of Heaven, where he watches over the weapons of the celestial armies. In later folklore, his image is so ubiquitous on swords and halberds that he has become a kind of spiritual presence embedded in the act of combat itself: when a warrior draws a blade, Yazi is already there, whispering the memory of every wound that blade has ever given.

His eventual fate is not recorded in any clear chronicle. In one quiet reading, he simply continues — a god without end, a grudge without closure, the eternal guardian of sharp edges. He does not liberate the yao race. He does not leave a legacy for his kin. He leaves only an image: a jackal-headed dragon, carved in jade, in iron, in gold, looking out from the hilt of a sword, his eyes promising that every blow will be answered.
body.body_10: Yazi's most enduring legacy is not a physical ruin but a cultural one. The idiom "睚眦必报" (yazi must repay) — meaning that even a glare will be avenged — is a direct reference to his nature. His image is preserved on countless ancient Chinese swords, some of which survive in museum collections, their hilts still bearing the unmistakable shape of the jackal-headed dragon. There is no single location associated with his deeds. His footprint is on the weapon, not on the land.
body.body_11: The entry on Yazi intersects with several other beings in this encyclopedia. Most directly, it connects to his father and elder brother among the Nine Sons of the Dragon, and to his sworn brother the Bull Demon King (Ni Mo Wang), who shares a similar history of defiance against the Heavenly Court. Yazi's service as the Celestial Blade-God also links him to Sun Wukong (Sun Wukong), who wielded a weapon bearing Yazi's likeness during his rebellion, sealing a symbolic connection between the stone monkey and the dragon-born god of vengeance.

guide.guide_1:
Imagine you're a dragon prince. Not the kind who flies around hoarding gold, but the kind whose father rules the Eastern Sea itself — a god older than most mountains. You're born powerful, majestic, with a jackal's head that can crush a warship's hull. And one day, as a child, you eat a piece of fruit your father was saving. Not a kingdom-destroying act, not a betrayal — just a kid being a kid. And your father, the King of Dragons, slaps you so hard he breaks one of your horns.

You don't cry for long. But you make a decision that day that you will never, ever take back. You stop looking him in the eye. Not out of fear. Out of the coldest, most patient form of spite you can imagine. And you carry that grudge. Not for a week. Not for a year. For eternity.

That's Yazi. That's the god of swords, the dragon-born whose name became a verb for getting even over the smallest slight. This is not a story about a demon. It's a story about what happens when the most powerful being in your world breaks your trust, and you decide to become the living monument of that break.
guide.guide_2:
If you've ever seen a Chinese sword — not the straight double-edged kind, but the curved blade that sings through the air — you've probably seen Yazi. His face is carved into the hilts, the scabbards, the cross-guards. He's the snarling dragon-head that guards the edge. And most people who buy those swords don't know his name. They just think it looks fierce.

He's one of the Nine Sons of the Dragon — a list of nine mythical creatures that the Dragon King supposedly fathered, each with its own specialty. Bixi carries stone tablets. Chiwen perches on roofs. And Yazi? Yazi is the one who kills. The one who remembers. The one who never forgets a debt of blood.

The simplified story is that he became the god of blades because he loves violence. But that's like saying a man thrown into a forge loves fire. The violence chose him, shaped him, became him. And it all started with a broken horn and a father who never apologized.
guide.guide_3:
So let's talk about Yazi's awakening to sentience — his Qi Zhi. And here's the thing: it doesn't look like the classic Yao awakening. He didn't crawl out of mud and suddenly realize he was thinking. He was born thinking. Dragon princes are born knowing the weight of their own blood. The moment he opened his jackal eyes, he already understood hierarchy, power, and that his father was the absolute ruler of everything he could see.

But knowledge without wisdom is a dangerous thing. And the Dragon King's cruelty taught Yazi exactly one lesson: love can be revoked. Trust can be shattered. The only safe emotion is the one that never expects anything in return. In a sense, Yazi's story is Kafka's *Metamorphosis* turned inside out: he was never a man who became an insect. He was an insect born into the body of a god, and the only way he could keep from being crushed was to become something harder than his father's claws. But the difference is crucial: in the Eastern telling, there is no tragic empathy for Yazi. He is not misunderstood — he is simply the thing he became. Cold. Exact. Unforgiving. And that is both his crime and his nature.
guide.guide_4:
Here's where Yazi's story gets weird, because he doesn't really go through the standard Yao grind. Most Yao — the fox spirits, the serpent queens, the tree-roots that crawl out of the earth — have to build their power from scratch. They eat moonlight that cuts their organs. They swallow other beasts' cores and hope the energies don't explode. They break their own bones, decade after decade, just to form a vaguely human skeleton.

Yazi never had to do any of that. He's a dragon's son. His core is dragon-vein pure. His body was already fit for cultivation from birth. He was given a path that other Yao would trade ten lifetimes for.

And the irony? He never wanted it. He didn't ask to be born the rightful prince of the Eastern Sea. He didn't ask to have power that cost him nothing. What he wanted was something he could never be given: an apology from his father. That never came. So he took the world's second-best prize — absolute authority over every blade, every sword-edge, every wound. It's not a Faustian bargain. Faust knew what he was giving up. Yazi gave up nothing and gained nothing. He just stood very still and let time hollow him out into a perfect weapon. And a weapon, as they say, cannot forgive.
guide.guide_5:
Now, the real question: if Yazi is the god of blades, why does he never use his power to do anything? He doesn't conquer kingdoms. He doesn't wage war. He just sits on the Dragon King's treasury, never looking at his father, watching the centuries slide past like a river.

Most readers understand this as a form of cosmic paralysis. Yazi is not a doer — he is a reminder. His entire existence is a monument to the one injury that broke him. He doesn't need to act because his mere presence is an accusation. Every time the Dragon King sees his second son's averted gaze, he knows exactly what he did. And that, for Yazi, is vengeance enough.

Is this a satisfying existence? No. It's a deeply broken one. But that's the point of the Yazi myth: not every wound heals. Not every father learns to say sorry. Not every son learns to forgive. Some people just become very quiet and very patient, and they wait for the world to catch up to their sorrow. Yazi is the god of that kind of waiting. He is the patron saint of the still, sullen grudge. And there is a kind of terrible poetry in that.
guide.guide_6:
Yazi's relationships are, to put it mildly, a mess. His father is the Dragon King, the ruler of the Eastern Sea, and the man who broke his horn. They haven't spoken in millennia. Not because they can't, but because Yazi refuses. Imagine Thanksgiving dinner that never ends, and you're always the person at the table refusing to make eye contact.

The Heavenly Court gave Yazi the title of "God of Blades" — a job, a role, a cage. It's not an honor. It's a leash. Heaven understood that Yazi was too dangerous to leave untethered. A dragon-born with a personal vendetta and no direction is a natural disaster. So they gave him a desk. A purpose. A way to channel his rage into something that served the celestial order rather than threatening it.

And the thing that's often glossed over is the sheer loneliness of it. Yazi is surrounded by people — his father, his seven other siblings, the celestial bureaucrats — but he is never *with* them. He is the brother who sits at the edge of the room. The official who does his job and disappears. The god who is present but never seen. If there is one relationship that defines him, it is the one he hasn't had: a single, honest, face-to-face conversation with his father, where the silence is not a weapon.
guide.guide_7:
So what do we do with a god who is defined by his refusal to forgive? In a Western frame, he might be a variation on the vengeful deity — Zeus with a thunderbolt, Odin brooding over a prophecy. But the Chinese Yazi is not a god who will be redeemed. There is no Ragnarök waiting for him, no final act where he lays down his grudge and becomes something greater.

And that, I think, is the reason his story endures. It is not a story about a monster. It is a story about what it costs to hold on. Yazi is not remembered for his power, his battles, or his conquests. He is remembered for his stillness. For the averted gaze. For the scar he chose not to heal.

In a world that tells us to let go, to forgive, to move on — Yazi is a stubborn, ancient voice saying: no. Some wounds should not be forgotten. Some betrayals should not be absolved. And if that leaves you alone on a throne of your own silence, so be it. He is not a model for living well. He is a mirror for the part of us that has ever been wronged and refused to let it go. And in that mirror, we see something uncomfortably familiar. The grudge. The silence. The scar we keep.

Maybe the real point of the Yao Saga is not to teach us how to become gods. It is to show us that gods are not so different from us. They, too, are broken by love. They, too, cannot always forgive.

lore_entries.surface_form: Long Sheng Jiu Zi (龙生九子)
lore_entries.description: The Nine Sons of the Dragon; the nine mythological offspring of the Dragon King, each with distinct powers and personalities, including Bixi, Chiwen, and Yazi.
Divine Weapons; swords, spears, and other edged weapons believed to be infused with Yazi's vengeful spirit and used in celestial warfare.

lore_entries.surface_form: Dao Jian Zhi Shen (刀剑之神)
lore_entries.description: The God of Blades and Swords; the celestial title granted to Yazi by the Heavenly Court, formalizing his connection to all sharp weaponry.
"Even a glare will be avenged"; a Chinese proverb directly derived from Yazi's nature, used to describe someone who is excessively vengeful over minor slights.

faq_entries.question: Is Yazi a demon or a monster?
faq_entries.answer: Neither. He is a Yao — a wild creature that awakened to sentience. But unlike most Yao, he is a dragon-born, the second son of the Dragon King, born with immense power rather than earning it through brutal cultivation.

faq_entries.question: Why is Yazi associated with swords?
faq_entries.answer: The Heavenly Court appointed him as the "God of Blades and Swords," partly as a containment strategy and partly because his image — a snarling jackal-headed dragon — became the standard decoration for weapons. A sword bearing his likeness was believed to possess his thirst for vengeance.

faq_entries.question: What is Yazi's most famous legend?
faq_entries.answer: His most defining story is the broken horn. As a cub, he ate a celestial fruit his father was saving. The Dragon King struck him so hard he shattered one of his horns. Yazi never forgave him, never looked him in the eye again, and carried the grudge for eternity.

faq_entries.question: Does Yazi have a human form like other Yao?
faq_entries.answer: No. Yazi retains his jackal-headed dragon-bodied form as his only shape. His refusal or inability to take on a full human form may be a statement — that he is not willing to be remade in the image of the beings who wronged him.

faq_entries.question: What is Yazi's current status?
faq_entries.answer: He is a Yao Saint, the highest level of Yao cultivation. He holds the title of God of Blades in the Heavenly Court and is primarily known as the decorative inspiration for swords and other edged weapons. He remains a solitary figure, still defined by the thousand-year-old grudge against his father.
